title: Full-disk encryption: BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS
quick: Full-disk encryption scrambles everything on a volume so it can only be read with the right key. BitLocker, FileVault and LUKS are the common systems on Windows, Mac and Linux.

sections.title: The idea
text: The system encrypts all data on the volume as it is written and decrypts it as it is read. An image of a locked volume contains only unreadable data. Without the key you cannot see files, file systems or deleted data.
The volume is encrypted with a main key. That key is itself protected by a password, a hardware module or a recovery key. The keys are therefore the first thing an examiner looks for.

sections.title: The three systems
text: BitLocker (Windows) can use a TPM, a chip that holds keys and checks the boot state, together with a PIN or startup key. It also has a recovery password that may be saved to a Microsoft account or a company directory.

FileVault (macOS) protects Mac volumes with AES-XTS. A recovery key is created when it is turned on. LUKS (Linux) keeps a header with keyslots. Each keyslot holds a copy of the master key protected by one passphrase or key. If the header is damaged, the data cannot be decrypted, so back it up.

sections.title: Practical steps
text: First find out if a volume is encrypted, and whether the system is running. A live running system may have keys in memory, and procedures differ by agency and country, so follow your lab's own procedure before powering anything off.

Look for recovery keys in accounts, directory services, printed pages or files, as the case allows. Document the state you found and every action you take. Guessing passwords is a separate and often slow task.

example: A laptop arrives powered off. The image shows an unreadable volume with a BitLocker marker. The case file lists a Microsoft account, and the investigator is authorised to request the recovery password through the proper channel. With it, the volume can be unlocked on a copy.
mistakes: Powering off a running system before checking for keys in memory.
Imaging only the unlocked drive and forgetting the original encrypted image.
Forgetting to back up a LUKS header before testing.
Assuming a strong password cannot be found elsewhere, such as in a stored recovery key.

exam.q: Why is a live system important when encryption is present?
exam.a: The volume is already unlocked and keys may be in memory. Powering off could make the data unreadable.

exam.q: Where might a BitLocker recovery password be stored?
exam.a: In a Microsoft account, in Active Directory or Entra ID, on a printout or in a saved file.
